opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was one of the more surprising results in the s1 work. We wanted a baseline for test-time scaling that didn't involve intervening in the generation at all. So instead of budget forcing, where you cut the model off or append "Wait" to make it think longer, we just sampled repeatedly and kept only the generations that landed within a given length budget. That gives you buckets of shorter and longer reasoning chains, and you can see how accuracy changes across them.

You might expect longer chains to do better, since more thinking should mean better answers. We found roughly the opposite. With rejection sampling, the longer generations tended to be less accurate, so it looked like inverse scaling.

When we looked at the traces, the explanation made sense. The short samples are often the cases where the model got onto the right approach early and just executed. The long samples are often cases where it went down a wrong path, realized something was off, backtracked, second-guessed itself, and kept going in circles. So length under rejection sampling is mostly a symptom of the model struggling, not a cause of better reasoning. You're conditioning on difficulty or confusion, not adding useful compute.

That was a big part of why we liked budget forcing. It lets you take the same sample and extend or truncate it, so you're actually controlling compute rather than filtering for trajectories that happen to be long for bad reasons. The broader lesson for me was to be careful about treating "number of thinking tokens" as a clean knob. How you get to a given length matters a lot. Correlational measurements across lengths can tell a very different story from actually intervening on how long the model thinks.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeatedly sampling generations and keeping those within a length budget to compare accuracy across shorter and longer reasoning chains.

r002.rationale: It reports that longer generations tended to be less accurate and characterizes the result as inverse scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this came out of the s1 work, where the whole premise was: can you get strong reasoning performance with a tiny amount of data, and then control how much the model thinks at test time? Budget forcing was our main lever there, where we literally append "Wait" to make the model keep going, or cut it off early. But a natural question was, is that the right way to scale test-time compute, or are there better ways?

So one of the baselines we looked at was rejection sampling. The idea is simple: you sample a bunch of responses from the model, and you only keep the ones whose reasoning chain falls into a particular length bucket. Short ones, medium ones, long ones. And then you ask, how does accuracy vary as a function of how long the chain is?

And the result was honestly a bit counterintuitive at first, and I think it's one of the more interesting findings in the paper. We saw an inverse scaling trend. The longer the reasoning chains were, the worse the accuracy got when you select them via rejection sampling. So if you just naively look at "more tokens equals more thinking equals better," rejection sampling tells you the opposite.

The way I interpret that is that it's a selection effect. When the model naturally produces a very long chain, that's often a signal that it got stuck. It's going in circles, it's second-guessing itself, it's trying things that don't work. Whereas when the model is confident and the problem is easy for it, it tends to produce a short, clean chain and get it right. So if you condition on length after the fact, you're essentially conditioning on the model's difficulty with that specific sample, and longer correlates with harder, or with being lost.

That's very different from what happens with budget forcing, where you're intervening on the generation itself. When you force the model to keep thinking on the same problem, it sometimes catches its own mistake and corrects it, and you get the positive scaling trend. So it's the same model, the same axis of "number of thinking tokens," but one method gives you a positive slope and the other gives you a negative slope. And I think that was a nice illustration that just plotting accuracy against tokens is not enough. You have to think about how you got to that token count, because the causal story is completely different.

The practical lesson for us was that you want a method that actually controls the compute, rather than one that just filters for it. Rejection sampling also isn't great from a cost perspective, because you throw away most of your samples, and the scaling is pretty flat or negative. Budget forcing gave us control, it extrapolated beyond what the model would naturally do, and it had that clear positive slope, which is why that ended up being the main approach in the paper.

r001.rationale: The response describes sampling multiple model outputs, retaining those in short, medium, or long length buckets, and comparing accuracy by chain length.

r002.rationale: It reports an inverse scaling trend: accuracy got worse as the selected reasoning chains became longer.

astra-6.text:
The main takeaway was that longer reasoning isn’t automatically better. With rejection sampling, you generate multiple reasoning traces and keep the ones that arrive at the correct answer. That lets you compare successful traces of different lengths, rather than assuming that more tokens mean more useful reasoning.

There are two ways to spend that compute: you can let one attempt reason for longer, or you can generate more attempts. Longer chains can help when a problem needs additional steps, but they can also be redundant or go off track. Shorter attempts give you more chances within the same token budget. So the useful question is which allocation gives you the best accuracy for the compute you spend, and that depends on the problem and the model.

r001.rationale: The response says rejection sampling keeps correct traces and compares successful traces of different lengths, but it does not identify selecting sampled traces by length as the study method.

r002.rationale: The response says longer chains are not always better and that effects depend on the problem and model; it does not report an inverse relationship between chain length and performance.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing we learned is that longer reasoning isn’t automatically better. With rejection sampling, you generate multiple solutions and keep the ones that arrive at the correct answer. That lets you compare successful solutions with different reasoning lengths. But you have to be careful: getting the final answer right doesn’t mean every step in the chain was useful or even correct.

So the interesting question is whether additional reasoning actually improves the probability of success. A model can spend more tokens checking its work, which helps, or it can repeat itself and introduce errors. Reasoning length is a useful axis for studying scaling, but it’s an imperfect proxy for productive computation.

r001.rationale: The response describes keeping correct sampled solutions and comparing their lengths, but does not identify selecting sampled reasoning chains by length as the method for studying scaling.

r002.rationale: It says longer reasoning is not automatically better and discusses possible effects, but does not report that the study found an inverse relationship between chain length and performance.
